assertions.observed:
WHAT IANA SAYS ABOUT RESERVED DOMAINS

Exact source URL (as requested): https://www.iana.org/domains/reserved
Page title: "IANA-managed Reserved Domains"

Key statements published by IANA on that page:

1. General framing / overview:
   "Certain domains are set aside, and nominally registered to 'IANA', for specific policy or technical purposes."

2. Example (documentation) domains:
   "As described in RFC 2606 and RFC 6761, a number of domains such as example.com and example.org are maintained for documentation purposes. These domains may be used as illustrative examples in documents without prior coordination with us. They are not available for registration or transfer."
   - Supporting RFC links given on the page: RFC 2606 ("Reserved Top Level DNS Names") and RFC 6761 ("Alternative Usage of the IETF Stream and Its Subtypes"), i.e. the RFCs that define reserved/special-use domain names.
   - IANA also links its IDN Evaluation / ICANN-related material in the adjacent paragraph on that page.

3. Policy-reserved domains and IANA's role:
   "We act as both the registrant and registrar for a select number of domains which have been reserved under policy grounds. These exclusions are typically indicated in either technical standards (RFC documents), or contractual limitations."
   - The phrase "contractual limitations" is a hyperlink on the page (pointing to IANA's contractual/agreement material), and the RFC references link to the IETF RFC documents.

In short, IANA states that reserved domains are names deliberately set aside (nominally registered to IANA) for policy or technical reasons; the "example" TLDs such as example.com/example.org (per RFC 2606 and RFC 6761) are reserved purely for documentation use, may be used illustratively in documents without coordinating with IANA, and are NOT available for registration or transfer; and for a select set of policy-reserved domains IANA serves as both registrant and registrar, with those exclusions defined either by technical standards (RFCs) or by contractual limitations.

**What asyncio is used for (per its official Python documentation page)**

Source URL (exact): https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio.html — page title: "asyncio — Asynchronous I/O — Python 3.14.7 documentation" (docs.python.org, the official Python documentation site).

Purpose, as stated on the page:
1. **Concurrent code via async/await** — "asyncio is a library to write concurrent code using the async/await syntax."
2. **Foundation for other async frameworks** — "asyncio is used as a foundation for multiple Python asynchronous frameworks that provide high-performance network and web-servers, database connection libraries, distributed task queues, etc."
3. **Best-fit workload** — "asyncio is often a perfect fit for IO-bound and high-level structured network code."

High-level APIs it provides (verbatim bullets from the page), to:
- run Python coroutines concurrently and have full control over their execution;
- perform network IO and IPC;
- control subprocesses;
- distribute tasks via queues;
- synchronize concurrent code.

For introspection, it provides APIs for:
- inspecting the async call graph of tasks and futures;
- inspecting tasks in another running Python process with command-line tools.

Low-level capability:
- "create and manage event loops, which provide asynchronous APIs for networking, running subprocesses, handling [OS/POSIX] signals…" (the event-loop bullet continues in the same sentence on the page).

Typical usage pattern shown on the page (the "Hello World!" example): define a coroutine and drive it with the runner, e.g. `async def main(): ... await asyncio.sleep(1) ...` then `asyncio.run(main())`.

Page structure (documented sub-areas of the library): High-level APIs (Runners, Coroutines and tasks, Streams, Synchronization Primitives, Subprocesses, Queues, Exceptions); Introspection APIs (Call graph introspection, Command-line introspection tools); Low-level APIs (Event loop, Futures, Transports and Protocols, Policies, Platform Support, Extending); plus Guides and Tutorials (High-level API Index, Low-level API Index, Developing with asyncio, asyncio and free-threaded Python). It sits under "Networking and Interprocess Communication" in the Python Standard Library docs.

In short: asyncio is Python's official library for writing asynchronous, concurrent code with `async`/`await`, mainly for IO-bound and structured network programs — powering network/IPC handling, subprocess control, task queues, synchronization primitives, and event-loop management, and serving as the base layer for many third-party async frameworks and servers.

**Role of Playwright locators (per the official Playwright for Python API reference)**

**Definition / core role:** The Locator class page states verbatim: *"Locators are the central piece of Playwright's auto-waiting and retry-ability. In a nutshell, locators represent a way to find element(s) on the page at any moment. A locator can be created with the `page.locator()` method."*

So a locator's role is to be a **lazy, reusable description of how to find elements**, not a captured element handle:

1. **Deferred resolution ("at any moment").** Creating a locator performs no DOM lookup and does not fail if nothing matches yet. The selector is re-evaluated each time the locator is used, so it always resolves against the *current* page state — this is what makes it safe across navigation, re-renders, and dynamic DOM changes (unlike a one-time `query_selector()` element handle that can go stale).

assertions.observed:
**What `git clone` does — per the official Git manual page (git-clone(1))**

**Primary source (exact URL):** https://git-scm.com/docs/git-clone — page title: "Git - git-clone Documentation"

**NAME section (as stated in the manual):**
> `git-clone` - Clone a repository into a new directory

**DESCRIPTION section (verbatim from the manual):**
1. "Clones a repository into a newly created directory, creates remote-tracking branches for each branch in the cloned repository (visible using `git branch --remotes`), and creates and checks out an initial branch that is forked from the cloned repository’s currently active branch."
2. "After the clone, a plain `git fetch` without arguments will update all the remote-tracking branches, and a plain `git pull` without arguments will in addition merge the remote master branch into the current master branch, if any (this is untrue when `--single-branch` is given; see below)."
3. "This default configuration is achieved by creating references to the remote branch heads under `refs/remotes/origin` and by initializing `remote.origin.url` and `remote.origin.fetch` configuration variables."

**Plain-language summary of those points:**
- `git clone` copies an existing repository (local path or a URL) into a **brand-new directory** that Git creates for you — it is a full copy, not just a checkout of the latest files: the whole history comes along.
- Inside the new directory it sets up **remote-tracking branches** — one for each branch that exists in the source repository — which you can list with `git branch --remotes`.
- It **creates and checks out an initial working branch** (by default `master`/`main`, i.e. `HEAD`) pointing at the source repository's currently active branch, so you can start working immediately.
- It wires up the new repo's relationship to the source: references to the remote's branch heads are stored under `refs/remotes/origin`, and the config variables `remote.origin.url` and `remote.origin.fetch` are initialized. Because of this, later plain `git fetch` updates all remote-tracking branches and plain `git pull` additionally merges the remote's default branch into the local one (except with `--single-branch`, where that tracking is limited).
- The manual's SYNOPSIS shows the command form `git clone [--template=<template-directory>] [-l] [-s] [--no-hardlinks] [-q] [-n] [--bare] [--mirror] [-o <name>] [-b <name>] ... <repository> [<directory>]`, i.e. behavior can be modified with options such as `--bare`, `--mirror`, `--depth`, `--single-branch`, `--recurse-submodules`, and `-b <name>` to check out a specific branch instead of the remote's default.

**What `git status` shows (per the official Git manual)**

**Name / purpose:** `git-status - Show the working tree status` (NAME section). Synopsis: `git status [<options>] [--] [<pathspec>…​]`.

"Effective Go" is the Go project's official style-and-idioms guide: a document that explains how to write programs that are not merely valid Go, but *good*, idiomatic Go.
